Clinical text (dates: 220080 to 220090): --- === Clinical Note dated 220080 === **PATHOLOGY REPORT** --- ### PATIENT INFORMATION **Name:** Margaret O'Connor  **MRN:** [Redacted]  **DOB:** [Redacted] ### SPECIMEN IDENTIFICATION | Accession # | Date of Collection* | |-------------|----------------------| | 2025‑001234 | — | \*Exact collection date omitted per instruction; will be inserted electronically. ### CLINICAL HISTORY & INDICATION Diagnosed cutaneous malignant melanoma of the left lower leg (proximal calf). Staging work‑up suggested regional nodal involvement; therefore a wide‑local excision (WLE) with concurrent sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) was performed. ### TYPE OF SPECIMEN 1. **Wide‑Local Excision (Skin):** Left lower leg, encompassing the pigmented lesion with surrounding normal skin. 2. **Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy:** Three axially oriented inguinal sentinel nodes obtained via intraoperative gamma probe guidance. ### GROSS DESCRIPTION #### Skin WLE - Received in formalin, labeled “Left Lower Leg Lesion”. - Elliptical segment measuring **3.2 cm × 2.1 cm × 0.9 cm** (length × width × depth). - Peripheral margin inks applied (dark blue). - Upon bisection, a central ulcerated area (~0.7 cm diameter) exposing underlying dermis was evident. - A firm, tan-pink nodule palpable beneath the ulcer extending to a maximal vertical height of **5.8 mm**, correlating with the deepest point of invasive component. - Remainder of specimen composed of unremarkable epidermis and subcutaneous fat. Tissue entirely submitted in serial sections. #### Sentinel Nodes (×3) - Each node individually cassetted, labelled SN‑01, SN‑02, SN‑03. - Sizes: 0.9 cm, 0.8 cm, and 0.7 cm greatest dimension respectively. - Bisected longitudinally; representative slices embedded in paraffin. ### MICROSCOPIC DIAGNOSIS 1. **Primary Cutaneous Melanoma** – *Superficial Spreading/Nodular type* - Invasive component measures **5.8 mm** Breslow thickness. - Ulceration present (full‑thickness epidermal loss overlying tumour). - Mitotic activity **12/mm²** (high). - Clark Level **IV/V** (deep infiltration into reticular dermis/subcutis). - No evidence of lymphovascular invasion. - Surgical margins: Deep margin uninvolved (>2 mm clearance); peripheral radial margins free of tumour (closest distance 1 mm). 2. **Sentinel Lymph Node Metastasis** - **SN‑01:** Metastatic deposit measuring **3.2 mm** in greatest dimension, confined to subcapsular sinus without capsular breach. - **SN‑02:** Metastatic focus **2.5 mm**, similar distribution; no extranodal extension. - **SN‑03:** Negative for malignancy. 3. **Immunohistochemistry (selected)** - **S‑100:** Strong diffuse nuclear/cytoplasmic positivity in both primary and nodal lesions. - **SOX10:** Positive confirming melanocytic lineage. - **HMB‑45/Melan‑A:** Focal cytoplasmic staining in primary tumour; weaker in nodal foci. - **Ki‑67:** Proliferative index ≈ 35 % in primary tumour; ≈ 25 % in nodal metastases. ### ANCEILLARY STUDIES No molecular assays were performed on this slide set at the time of reporting. Formalin‑fixed material has been retained for potential downstream Next‑Generation Sequencing per treating physician request (subsequent report dated separately). ### PATHOLOGIC STAGE (AJCC 8th Edition) - **pT3b** – Tumour >4 mm thick with ulceration. - **pN2a** – Metastasis in 2–3 regional nodes, none >2 cm in greatest dimension, without extranodal extension. - **cM0** – Clinically no distant metastasis identified at time of surgery. Overall pathological stage: **Stage IIIB** (resectable disease at presentation). ### COMMENT (Reserved for optional technical comment; none required.) --- **Signed:** _______________________________ **Dr. Jane E. Pathologist, MD** Board Certified Anatomic Pathology Date Report Finalized: — *(Electronic signature)* === Clinical Note dated 220081 === **Next‑Generation Sequencing Report – Comprehensive Genomic Profiling** --- ### Patient Information **Name:** Margaret O'Connor  **Sex/Age:** Female / 70 years ### Specimen Details | Item | Description | |--------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------| | **Specimen Identifier** | SLX‑001‑LM‑070 | | **Source** | Formalin‑fixed, paraffin‑embedded (FFPE) block from wide‑local excision of left lower‑leg melanoma (primary skin lesion) | | **Date Received** | [date withheld] | | **Tumor Content** | Estimated ≥30% neoplastic cells (H&E review) | ### Test Performed Comprehensive solid‑tumor panel covering >300 cancer‑relevant genes (DNA‐based hybrid‑capture NGS). ### Patient & Specimen Identification

### Test Overview  
- **Assay Platform:** Hybrid‑capture DNA next‑generation sequencing panel targeting >300 cancer‐related genes, selected introns for rearrangement detection, and genome‑wide copy‑number evaluation.  
- **Sequencing Metrics:** Mean unique read depth = 750×; minimum coverage ≥100× across >99 % of target bases. Analytic sensitivity ≤5 % allele frequency for single nucleotide variants/indels; copy‑number calls reliable down to 4‑copy gain.  
- **DNA Input:** 150 ng extracted from macrodissected tumor area.  

### Detected Genomic Alterations  

| Gene | Variant (HGVS) | Classification* | Allelic Fraction (%) | Type |
|------|----------------|------------------|-----------------------|------|
| **TP53** | NM_000546.5:c.524G>A (p.Arg175His) | Likely pathogenic (hotspot) | 48 | Missense SNV |
| **BRCA1** | NM_007294.3:c.5946+1G>A (splice donor) | Pathogenic | 42 | Splice‑site alteration |
| **CCNE1** | Copy‑Number Gain – estimated 7‑fold increase (CN ≈14) | Potentially clinically significant | — | Amplication |
| **KRAS** | NM_004985.5:c.35G>T (p.Gly12Val) | Low‑frequency subclone (likely passenger) | 4 | Missense SNV |

\*Classification follows ACMG/AMP guidelines and internal oncology laboratory criteria.

#### Additional Findings  
- **Microsatellite Status:** Stable (MSI‑Stable) – evaluated via mononucleotide repeat markers incorporated in the panel.  
- **Tumor Mutation Burden (TMB):** 3.2 mutations/Mb (low).  
- **Other Genes Assessed:** No pathogenic or likely pathogenic alterations detected in ERBB2, PIK3CA, PTEN, AKT1, NF1, STK11, or HRR pathway members besides BRCA1. No gene fusions identified.  

### Interpretive Summary  

1. **TP53 p.R175H** – This missense substitution occurs at a well‑characterized DNA‑binding domain hotspot and confers loss of normal p53 tumor suppressor function. It is virtually universal in high‑grade serous ovarian carcinoma and supports the diagnosis.  

2. **BRCA1 splice‑site mutation (c.5946+1G>A)** – Predicted to disrupt canonical splicing leading to truncated protein product and homologous recombination deficiency (HRD). - **Assay:** Hybrid capture–based comprehensive solid tumor DNA panel covering >300 cancer‐relevant genes (including SNVs, indels, copy‑number alterations, selected fusions).  
- **Platform:** Illumina NovaSeq 6000, paired‑end 150 bp reads.  
- **Sequencing Depth:** Median unique depth ≥800× across target regions.  
- **Analytical Sensitivity:** Detects single nucleotide variants (SNV)/indels ≥5% VAF, copy‑number gains ≥4‑fold relative to diploid baseline, homozygous deletions when both alleles absent.  
- **Quality Metrics:** All QC parameters met acceptance criteria (≥95% bases >Q30, uniformity >90%).  

### Detected Genomic Alterations  

| Gene | Variant(s) | Molecular Consequence | Allele Frequency* | Interpretation |
|------|------------|-----------------------|-------------------|---------------|
| **SMARCA4** | *Biallelic deletion* (exons 1‑31 lost) | Loss of function → SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex disruption | — (copy‑neutral loss) | Consistent with SMARCA4‑deficient (“SWI/SNF‑mut”) thoracic adenocarcinoma; associated with aggressive phenotype. |
| **KRAS** | c.35G>A (p.G12D) | Activating missense mutation | 38% | Classic KRAS driver; predicts resistance to EGFR‑directed TKIs. |
| **STK11** | c.1060T>C (p.F354L) | Predicted loss‑of‑function (LOF) | 32% | Co‑mutation with KRAS linked to poorer outcomes and reduced responsiveness to PD‑1 blockade. |
| **NF1** | c.4724A>T (p.Q1575H) | Likely pathogenic missense (loss of RAS GAP activity) | 27% | Contributes to MAPK pathway activation. |
| **MET** | Copy‑Number Amplification ≈7‑fold increase (relative to diploid control) | Overexpression/amplified signaling through HGF-MET axis | — | High‑level amplification (>5‑fold) potentially actionable with MET inhibitors. |

\*Allele frequency represents proportion of mutated reads among total informative reads after correction for tumor cellularity (~60% estimated).

### Interpretative Commentary  

1. **Oncogenic Drivers** – The tumor harbors multiple activating alterations in the Ras/Raf/MEK pathway (KRAS G12D, NF1 loss, STK11 LOF). This constellation drives constitutive downstream signaling and underlies the observed aggressive behavior. Presence of KRAS G12D precludes efficacy of EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors.

2. **SMARCA4 Deficiency** – Complete loss of SMARCA4 protein correlates with “SMARCA4‑deficient” NSCLC, a subset characterized by high-grade morphology, propensity for early dissemination, and limited sensitivity to conventional chemotherapy.

3. **MET Amplification** – A seven‑fold gain exceeds most institutional cutoffs for potential MET‑targeted therapy (e.g., crizo, tepotinib, savolitinib). Confirmation via orthogonal method (e.g., FISH) is advisable before enrollment into MET‑focused trials.

4. **Co‑occurrence of KRAS & STK11** – Evidence suggests diminished benefit from anti‑PD‑1/PD-L1 monotherapies in KRAS‑mutant NSCLC harboring concurrent STK11 loss. Coupled with low TMB and MSS status, predictive markers favor modest immunotherapy responsiveness.

5. **TP53 Mutation** – While TP53 alterations are frequent in lung adenocarcinoma, they confer additional genomic instability but lack direct therapeutic implication outside investigational contexts.

### Limitations  

- The assay interrogates DNA alterations only; RNA fusion partners were not assessed.  
- Subclonal populations below the detection threshold (<5% VAF) could remain undetected.  
- Functional impact of certain missense changes (e.g., STK11 F354L) inferred from computational predictions; confirmatory functional assays unavailable.

### Recommendations (Interpretation Only)

- Consider confirmation of MET amplification by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) or quantitative PCR.  
- Discuss suitability for clinical trial enrolment targeting KRAS G12D, MET amplification, or SMARCA4‑deficient cohorts.  
- Given the KRAS/STK11/TMB profile, anticipate limited benefit from single-agent PD‑1/PD‑L1 blockade; combination strategies may warrant exploration pending multidisciplinary discussion.

You are an expert cancer registrar extracting first course radiation treatment data.

TASK: Extract radiation therapy information. Include ONLY first course radiation treatment.

CRITICAL RULES:
1. RADIATION DATE: Date radiation therapy started (YYYYMMDD).
2. RX SUMM--RADIATION: 0=none, 1=beam radiation, 2=radioactive implants, 3=radioisotopes, 4=combination, 5=radiation NOS, 9=unknown.
3. RADIATION PHASES: Radiation may have up to 3 phases. Each phase has: dose per fraction, number of fractions, total dose, treatment modality, planning technique, treatment volume.

5. MODALITY: Photons, electrons, protons, IMRT, stereotactic, brachytherapy, etc.

7. For each item, rate confidence 0.0-1.0 and quote evidence.

The metastatic clear‑cell renal cell carcinoma harbors several canonical drivers characteristic of this histotype:

## Assessment  

1. **Metastatic clear‑cell renal cell carcinoma**, refractory to sequential VEGF‑targeted TKIs (sunitinib → axitinib). Molecular profile demonstrates VHL splice‑site alteration, multiple chromatin‐modifying gene losses (PBRM1, BAP1) and PTEN loss—all associated with aggressive biology and poorer response to checkpoint inhibition. Currently limited systemic options; enrollment in most active trials precluded by prior VEGF‑TKI exposure and rapid recurrence timeline.  

2. **Functional decline** – ECOG 2, increasing dependence on caregiver support, intermittent dyspnea, moderate fatigue, and psychosocial distress concerning prognosis.  

3. **Hepatic dysfunction** – Transaminases ≈2 × ULN, likely multifactorial (tumour infiltrative vs underlying hepatitis C sequelae). Limits tolerability of many systemic agents and influences anticoagulant metabolism.  

4. **Deep‑Vein Thrombosis** – On therapeutic enoxaparin; no bleeding complications thus far.  

5. **Hypertension** – Well-controlled on lisinopril; monitor closely if anti‑angiogenic therapy reinitiated.  

6. **Symptomatic burdens** – Diarrhea (residual from prior axitinib), mild nausea, hand‑foot skin toxicity largely resolved, anxiety/depressed mood.  

Overall goal shifts toward maximizing quality of life, alleviating symptoms, clarifying values/goals, and facilitating coordinated hospice planning if desired.

**A. Immediate Symptom Management**

=== Clinical Note dated 177113 ===
**PATHOLOGY REPORT**

---

### Specimen Identification  
- **Accession #:** BM‑00123456  
- **Patient:** Robert Chen, DOB [redacted]  
- **Age/Sex:** 68‑yr Male  
- **Site of Collection:** Posterior superior iliac spine, bone‐marrow aspirate & core biopsy  

### Date of Procedure  
(Exact calendar date omitted per protocol)

---  

## Gross Description  

**Bone‑Marrow Aspiration:** Two syringes of heparinized marrow obtained; total volume ≈ 2 mL. The aspirate appeared mildly turbid, cellular, without overt clots. Smears prepared immediately.

**Core Biopsy:** One trephine core measuring 2.0 cm in length × 0.6 cm diameter submitted in formalin. Fixed in neutral buffered formalin for 24 h, then decalcified briefly before processing. No macroscopic abnormality noted aside from expected trabecular architecture.

---  

## Microscopic Examination  

**Aspirate Smear Review (H&E, Wright–Giemsa):**  
- Markedly hypercellular marrow (>90 % cellularity).  
- Predominantly small to intermediate sized mononuclear cells with scant basophilic cytoplasm, round nuclei, fine chromatin, and inconspicuous nucleoli.  
- Approximate blast count = 85 % of nucleated elements. Occasional occasional Auer rods absent. Scattered mature erythroid precursors and megakaryocytes markedly decreased.  

**Core Biopsy (H&E):**  
- Diffuse infiltration by sheets of immature lymphoblasts replacing normal hematopoietic elements.  
- Nuclear molding and high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio evident.  
- No significant fibrosis; reticulin stain shows low-grade increase (MF‑1).  

Overall morphological impression: “Morphologically compatible with B‑lymphoblastic leukemic infiltrates.”

---  

## Ancillary Studies  

### Flow Cytometric Immunophenotyping (8‑color panel)  

| Antigen | Result |
|---------|--------|
| CD45    | Dim |
| CD19    | Positive (+) |
| CD20    | Negative (-) |
| CD22    | Variable + |
| CD10    | Positive (+) |
| CD34    | Positive (+) |
| TdT     | Positive (+) |
| CD79a   | Positive (+) |
| Surface IgM | Negative (-) |
| Kappa light chain restriction | Not detected |
| Lambda light chain restriction | Not detected |

*Interpretation:* Strong expression of early B‑lineage antigens (CD19, CD10, CD34, TdT) supports a diagnosis of precursor B‑cell lineage acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

### Molecular Analysis  

- **Reverse Transcriptase PCR (RT‑PCR) for BCR‑ABL1 Fusion Transcripts**  
  - Targeted assay for e1a2 (p190) transcript.  
  - *Result*: Detectable BCR‑ABL1 p190 fusion transcript; quantitative level approximately 15 % normalized copy number relative to control gene (ABL).  

- **Additional Molecular Panel (NGS)** – not ordered at this encounter; pending subsequent workup.

---  

## Diagnostic Summary  

1. **Acute B‑lymphoblastic leukaemia (B‑ALL),** WHO classification, characterized by >80 % blasts in marrow.  
2. **Philadelphia chromosome‑positive (Ph+)**, evidenced by presence of BCR‑ABL1 p190 fusion transcript by RT‑PCR.  
3. Immunophenotype: CD19⁺, CD10⁺, CD34⁺, TdT⁺, surface Ig−, confirming precursor B‑cell origin.  

These findings correlate with the clinical presentation of high‑grade Ph⁺ B‑ALL.

---  

## Comments  

- Specimens adequate for full morphologic, immunophenotypic, and molecular evaluation.  
- No evidence of myeloid differentiation or mixed phenotype disease on current panels.  
- Recommend correlation with cytogenetics/karyotype when available for comprehensive genomic profiling.  

*(Report generated by Department of Hematopathology)*

=== Clinical Note dated 177114 ===
**INSTITUTIONAL MOLECULAR PATHOLOGY SERVICE – CLINICAL GENOMIC REPORT**

---

### Patient Information  
**Name:** Robert Chen  **MRN:** [Redacted]  **Sex/Age:** Male / 68 y  

### Specimen Details  
| Item                     | Description                                 |
|--------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| **Specimen ID**          | BM‑001‑202X                                  |
| **Source**               | Bone marrow aspiration (sternal puncture)   |
| **Collection Date**      | *Date omitted – to be entered electronically* |
| **Received By Lab**       | Molecular Diagnostics Unit                  |

### Test Ordered  
Comprehensive Next‑Generation Sequencing (NGS) panel for hematologic malignancies covering DNA‐based mutation detection, copy number variation (CNV) analysis, RNA‑fusion discovery, and expression profiling (including CRLF2).

### Methodology Summary  
- **DNA & RNA extraction:** Automated magnetic bead–based isolation (Qiagen).  
- **Library preparation:** Hybrid‑capture enrichment (Illumina TruSight Oncology 500); separate cDNA synthesis for fusion/transcript quantification.  
- **Sequencing platform:** Illumina NovaSeq 6000, paired‑end 150 bp reads.  
- **Coverage statistics:** Median depth ≥ 800× across target regions; >99% bases covered at ≥30×.  
- **Bioinformatic pipeline:** Alignment to hg38, variant calling with Mutect2 (SNVs/indels), CNVkit (copy‑number), STAR‑Fusion (RNA fusions), normalized read count for gene expression.  
- **Analytical sensitivity:** Detectable allelic fraction ≥ 2% for SNVs/indels; ≥ 5% for structural variants.

### Genomic Findings  

| Alteration                              | Variant Class            | Allele Frequency* | Clinical Significance* |
|----------------------------------------|---------------------------|-------------------|-------------------------|
| **BCR‑ABL1 fusion (e13a2)**             | Gene Fusion (p190 protein) | Detected (RNA)    | Pathogenic – hallmark of Philadelphia‑positive ALL; confers constitutive ABL1 TK activity. |
| **IKZF1 exon 4‑7 deletion**            | Homozygous Deletion (CNV) | —                 | Adverse prognostic marker in Ph⁺ B‑ALL; linked to steroid resistance. |
| **CDKN2A/CDKN2B homozygous loss**       | Homozygous Deletion (CNV) | —                 | Tumor suppressor loss; associated with aggressive phenotype. |
| **CRLF2 overexpression**                | mRNA Upregulation         | ≈ 8‑fold ↑ vs normal control | Suggestive of JAK‑STAT pathway activation; seen in “Ph‑like” subset but co‑exists here. |
| **KRAS G12D**                           | Missense SNV              | 15%               | Activating MAPK pathway mutation; contributes to leukemogenesis. |
| **NRAS Q61K**                           | Missense SNV              | 9%                | Co‑occurring activating RAS mutation; similar functional impact as KRAS. |
| **PTPN11 E69K**                         | Missense SNV              | 6%                | Gain‑of‑function phosphatase affecting downstream signaling; reported in acute leukemia. |

\*Allele frequency reflects proportion of mutated reads among total informative reads (applicable to SNVs/Indels). Copy‑number changes are reported qualitatively.

### Interpretative Commentary  

The comprehensive genomic profile confirms classic Philadelphia chromosome positivity through detection of the BCR‑ABL1 p190 transcript, establishing the diagnosis of Ph⁺ B‑ALL. Concomitant IKZF1 deletion and biallelic loss of CDKN2A/B denote a high‑risk genetic backdrop frequently correlated with inferior response to standard chemotherapy regimens. Overexpression of CRLF2 raises the possibility of synergistic JAK‑STAT signaling, although no accompanying JAK2 rearrangement was observed.

Activating lesions in KRAS, NRAS, and PTPN11 collectively indicate robust MAPK pathway engagement, potentially contributing to disease persistence despite targeted ABL inhibition. While these RAS‑pathway mutations are less typical in isolated Ph⁺ cases, their presence underscores biologic heterogeneity and may influence future therapeutic considerations such as incorporation of MEK inhibitors—though such decisions lie outside the scope of this report.

Overall, the detected aberrations delineate a complex mutational landscape characteristic of high‑risk adult B‑ALL and provide essential baseline data for longitudinal minimal residual disease (MRD) tracking and potential enrollment into genotype‑directed clinical trials.

### Report Limitations  

- Sensitivity limited to ≥ 2% VAF for single nucleotide variants; subclonal events below this threshold may remain undetected.  
- Structural variations other than targeted fusions (e.g., cryptic insertions) are not comprehensively assessed.  
- Expression levels derived from bulk RNA; tumor purity influences quantitative accuracy.

Board‑Certified Molecular Geneticist

**Oncology Consultation Note – Initial Hematology–Oncologic Assessment**

---

### Patient Identifiers  
**Name:** Robert Chen  **Age:** 68  **Sex:** Male  

---  

#### Chief Complaint  
Newly diagnosed acute B‑cell lymphoblastic leukemia (B‑ALL); request for specialist evaluation and treatment planning.

---  

#### History of Present Illness  
Robert presented three weeks ago with progressive fatigue, easy bruising, and intermittent low‑grade fevers. Laboratory work‐up revealed marked leukocytosis (WBC 78 ×10⁹/L) with circulating lymphoblasts comprising approximately 85 % of nucleated cells. Peripheral smear confirmed abundant immature lymphoid precursors exhibiting scant cytoplasm, fine chromatin, and occasional prominent nucleoli.

Comprehensive staging investigations were undertaken:

=== Clinical Note dated 244417 ===
**Pathology Report**

**Patient:** Emily Carter  
**MRN:** ***[Redacted]***  

| **Report Number** | **Specimen ID**                     |
|-------------------|-------------------------------------|
| 2023‑01‑BR-045    | LEFT BREAST CORE NEEDLE BIOPSY #001 |

**Date of Procedure:** *Not Provided*  
**Date Received:** *Not Provided*  
**Date Finalized:** *Not Provided*

### SPECIMEN TYPE & SOURCE
Core needle biopsies obtained under ultrasound guidance from a palpable abnormality located in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast. Six cores were submitted in separate labeled containers (Cores A–F).

### GROSS DESCRIPTION
Received six cylindrical fragments of tan-white fibroadipose tissue measuring:

| Fragment | Length (mm) | Width (mm) |
|----------|-------------|------------|
| A        | 18          | 4          |
| B        | 16          | 3.5        |
| C        | 17          | 3.8        |
| D        | 15          | 3.2        |
| E        | 19          | 4.1        |
| F        | 14          | 3.0        |

Total aggregate length ≈ 99 mm. All specimens inked, fixed in neutral buffered formalin, processed routinely, embedded in paraffin, sectioned at 4 µm thickness, and stained with hematoxylin‑eosin (H&E). Additional unstained slides prepared for immunohistochemical (IHC) studies.

### MICROSCOPIC FINDINGS

#### Histologic Diagnosis
- Infiltrating (ductal) carcinoma, NST (No Special Type)
- Nottingham Grade 2 (tubule formation score 3, nuclear pleomorphism score 2, mitotic count score 2)

#### Morphology
Sections reveal malignant epithelial cells forming irregular glandular/tubular structures infiltrating desmoplastic stroma. Tumor cells display moderate cytological atypia with vesicular nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and occasional apocrine features. Mitotic activity approximates 5 per 10 HPFs. No necrosis observed. The surrounding adipose tissue shows focal fibrosis secondary to needle tract injury.

#### Margins / Extent
Tumor involvement extends throughout multiple cores; however, because the material consists solely of core samples, margin status cannot be assessed.

#### Lymphovascular/Invasion
No definitive lymphovascular invasion identified in examined levels.

### IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY (ANCILLARY STUDIES)

| Marker      | Method               | Result                               | Interpretation                         |
|--------------|----------------------|--------------------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| Estrogen Receptor (ER)   | Clone SP1, Ventana Benchmark Ultra | Positive – Nuclear staining in 95% of tumor cells, strong intensity (Allred Score 8) | Hormone‑responsive phenotype |
| Progesterone Receptor (PR) | Clone PgR636, Ventana Benchmark Ultra | Positive – Nuclear staining in 80% of tumor cells, moderate‑strong intensity (Allred Score 7) | Hormone‑responsive phenotype |
| HER2 (c-erbB‑2)           | Clone 4B5, Ventana BenchMark ULTRA (IHC) | Negative – Membranous staining absent (Score 0) | Not amplified; no anti‑HER2 targeted therapy indicated |
| Ki‑67                      | Clone MIB‑1, Leica Bond III            | Approximately 20% of tumor cell nuclei positively stained (low‑intermediate proliferative index) |
| Cytokeratin AE1/AE3       | Polyclonal, Dako Autostainer Link 48 | Diffuse strong positivity confirming epithelial nature |
| S100                       | Polycolonal, Dako                    | Negative – excludes melanoma/metaplastic component |

Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) for HER2 amplification was not performed owing to unequivocal IHC 0 result.

### MOLECULAR TESTING

### TEST PERFORMED
Comprehensive solid‑tumor genomic profiling utilizing a validated 511‑gene hybrid‑capture NGS panel (Commercially marketed as “OncoPanel‑511”). The assay interrogates coding regions of selected genes for base substitutions, insertions/deletions, select intronic fusions, copy‑number alterations, and limited structural rearrangements.

### METHODOLOGY SUMMARY
- Library preparation via enzymatic fragmentation & adapter ligation.  
- Target enrichment by biotinylated probe hybridization (median target coverage ≈ 550×).  
- Paired‑end sequencing on Illumina NovaSeq 6000.  
- Bioinformatic pipeline includes alignment to hg19, duplicate removal, local realignment, and variant calling (MuTect2 for SNVs/indels; CNVkit for copy‑number).  
- Variant annotation utilizes COSMIC v94, ClinVar, OncoKB, and internal curated database.  
- Analytical sensitivity: ≥5 % allelic fraction for SNVs/indels; ≥2‑copy fold change for amplifications; detection of homozygous deletions ≤1 % cellularity.

### RESULTS

#### Somatic Sequence Variants (Pathogenic / Likely Pathogenic)

| Gene | Nucleotide Change* | Protein Effect | Allele Frequency (%) | Classification |
|------|--------------------|---------------|---------------------|----------------|
| **PIK3CA** | c.3140A>G | p.His1047Arg | 27 | Pathogenic (activating) |
| **TP53**   | c.524G>T | p.Arg175His | 22 | Pathogenic (loss‑of‑function) |
| **CDH1**   | c.1799‑1G>A | Splice donor ‑1 → A (exon 13) | — | Likely pathogenic (disrupts E‑cadherin) |
| **GATA3**  | c.424_425delAG | p.Ser142Phefs*24 | 15 | Likely pathogenic (frameshift) |
| **ESR1**   | c.1610A>C | p.Tyr537Ser | 5 | Pathogenic (ligand‑binding domain mutation conferring hormone resistance) |
| **MAP3K1** | c.964G>A | p.Glu322Lys | 12 | Likely pathogenic (kinase domain) |

\*Genomic coordinates refer to NM_* transcripts according to RefSeq.

#### Copy‑Number Alterations

| Gene | Type | Approximate Fold Change |
|------|------|--------------------------|
| **CCND1** | Amplification | +4‑fold (high‑level) |
| **CDKN2A** | Homozygous Deletion | Loss of both alleles |
| **PTEN** | Low‑level loss | Relative copy number decrease (~−1.5 copies) |

#### Additional Findings
- No clinically significant BRCA1/BRCA2 somatic alterations detected.  
- No microsatellite instability (MSI‑stable) inferred from indel distribution.  
- Tumor mutational burden (TMB): 4 Mut/Mb (low).

### INTERPRETION
Emily’s tumor harbors several well‑characterized driver alterations typical of HR⁺/HER2‑negative breast cancer:

1. **PIK3CA H1047R** – Activating hotspot mutation driving PI3K‑AKT signaling; predictive of responsiveness to α‑specific PI3K inhibitors (e.g., alpelisib) when paired with endocrine therapy.  
2. **ESR1 Y537S** – Constitutively active ligand‑binding domain substitution associated with acquired resistance to aromatase inhibition; may influence choice of subsequent hormonal agents.  
3. **TP53 R175H**, **CDH1 splice-site**, **GATA3 frameshift**, and **MAP3K1 missense** collectively reflect genomic complexity and could contribute to altered differentiation and proliferative capacity.  
4. **CCND1 amplification** together with **CDKN2A loss** suggests dysregulation of cell‑cycle control (Cyclin D1–CDK4/6 axis). While not directly therapeutic without CDK4/6 inhibitor data, it aligns biologically with favorable responses seen with standard chemotherapy regimens.  
5. **Low‑level PTEN loss** further supports activation of the PI3K pathway.

Overall, the profile confirms a classic Luminal B‑like genotype despite low Ki‑67 on initial pathology, providing rationale for targeted strategies should progression occur.

### LIMITATIONS
- Testing performed on archival FFPE material; very low tumor purity (<10 %) could result in false negatives.  
- Intronic/rearrangement detection limited to predefined hotspots; novel fusion partners may be missed.  
- Germline status cannot be assessed; separate hereditary testing required if indicated.

No new musculoskeletal complaints.

### Technique
Whole‑body planar bone scintigraphy performed three hours after intravenous administration of **740 MBq (20 mCi)** technetium‑99m methylene diphosphonate (**Tc‑99m MDP**) intravenously. Anterior and posterior whole‑body images were obtained, supplemented by static spot views of the skull, cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine, pelvis, proximal femora, and selected regions of the extremities. Images were processed with standard matrix settings; count statistics were adequate.

### Findings

| Region | Observation |
|--------|-------------|
| **Skull & Cervical Spine** | Uniform physiological tracer distribution. No focal photopenic defects or focal intense uptake. Small symmetric occipital condyle activity compatible with normal growth plate remnants. |
| **Thoracic Spine** | Homogeneous vertebral body uptake. No lytic or blastic lesions identified. Mildly increased uptake at C7/T1 junction likely related to chronic mechanical stress. |
| **Lumbar Spine** | Physiological pattern throughout L1‑L5. Degenerative facet joint arthritis evident at L4‑L5 bilaterally with mildly increased marginal uptake—consistent with benign spondylosis. No focal “hot spots.” |
| **Ribs & Sternum** | Symmetric rib cage activity without focal abnormalities. No costochondritis or fracture signs. |
| **Pelvis & Sacrum** | Normal sacroiliac joint uptake. No pelvic lesions detected. Slightly increased activity over bilateral iliac crests correlates with muscular insertion sites – benign. |
| **Proximal Femora & Hip Joints** | Even tracer distribution. No avascular necrosis or metastatic foci observed. |
| **Upper Extremities** | Physiologic soft‑tissue background. No focal uptake in humeri, radius, ulna, or hands. |
| **Lower Extremities** | Moderate diffuse increase in tracer accumulation around both knees, most pronounced medially, reflecting underlying osteoarthritic change. No discrete lesions identified. |

Overall, there is **no abnormal focal radionuclide concentration** suggesting metastatic involvement of the skeleton. Incidental findings are limited to expected age‑related degenerative changes (lumbar facet arthropathy, bilateral knee osteoarthritis) and physiologic variants.

Clinical text (dates: 251165 to 251175): --- === Clinical Note dated 251165 === **PATHOLOGY REPORT** --- **Patient:** James Patel  **Age/Sex:** 68‑yr / Male **Accession #:** CP‑2023‑00127  **Specimen ID:** COLORECTAL‑BIOPSY‑A01 **Date of Procedure:** [date withheld] **Date Received:** [date withheld] **Date Reported:** [date withheld] ### CLINICAL HISTORY Radiologic evaluation demonstrates a 6.4 cm irregular mass arising from the ascending colon (right hemicolon) with adjacent lymphadenopathy (stations 12 and 13). An image‑guided core needle biopsy was obtained for tissue diagnosis. ### SPECIMEN DESCRIPTION *Procedure:* Percutaneous ultrasound‑guided core needle biopsy of the ascending colon mass. Four separate core specimens were submitted in formalin. *Gross Examination:* Four cylindrical cores, tan-white, firm, ranging from 0.8 cm to 1.2 cm in greatest dimension; cumulative linear measurement ≈ 4.5 cm. All cores inked circumferentially, bisected, processed routinely, embedded in paraffin, and stained with hematoxylin–eosin (H&E). Additional unstained slides prepared for potential ancillary studies. ### MICROSCOPIC FINDINGS #### Histopathology (H&E) - The sampled tissue reveals invasive carcinoma composed predominantly of markedly pleomorphic glands and sheets of single dispersed cells exhibiting classic *signet‑ring* morphology (large intracytoplasmic vacuoles displacing hyperchromatic nuclei to the periphery). - Tumor cells display scant cytoplasm, marked nuclear atypia, prominent nucleoli, and frequent mitoses (>15/10 HPF). - Infiltration extends through the lamina propria into the superficial muscularis propria; desmoplastic stromal reaction is evident. - Necrosis is focal (<10% of examined area). - No residual benign colonic epithelium identifiable in the limited sample. **Tumor Grading:** High‑grade (Grade III) poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma with signet‑ring cell features. #### Immunohistochemical Profile *(performed on representative block)* | Marker | Result | |--------|--------| | Cytokeratin 20 (CK20) | Diffuse strong positivity | | Caudal Type Homeobox 2 (CDX2) | Strong nuclear positivity | | Cytokeratin 7 (CK7) | Negative | | Mismatch Repair Proteins (MLH1, PMS2, MSH2, MSH6) | Retained nuclear expression in neoplastic cells | | Ki‑67 (MIB‑1) | Approximately 82 % labeling index | | HER2 (IHC) | Score 0 (negative) | All controls performed appropriately; interpretation concordant with colorectal origin and microsatellite stability. ### ANCESTRY STUDIES No molecular assays (e.g., targeted Next‑Generation Sequencing, KRAS/BRAF mutation testing) were ordered on this initial biopsy specimen. Slides are archived for optional reflex testing upon request. ### DIAGNOSTIC SUMMARY - **Primary Diagnosis:** Poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon, WHO grade III, with signet‑ring cell differentiation. - **Immunoprofile:** CK20⁺/CDX2⁺, CK7⁻, intact MMR protein expression (suggestive of microsatellite stable status), high proliferative activity (Ki‑67≈82 %). These morphologic and immunophenotypic characteristics support a biologically aggressive colorectal carcinoma. Further molecular characterization (e.g., KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, PIK3CA, TMB) is advisable for therapeutic decision‑making, though such testing falls outside the scope of this pathological evaluation. --- **Pathologist:** _________________________ **Signature:** _______________________ **Report Verified By:** ___________________ **Date:** ________________________ === Clinical Note dated 251166 === **Imaging Report** --- **Patient:** James Patel **Age/Sex:** 68‑year‑old Male **Study:** Baseline Contrast‑Enhanced Computed Tomography (CT) – Chest, Abdomen, and Pelvis **Indication:** Initial staging work‑up following diagnosis of newly biopsied ascending colon adenocarcinoma (grade 3, MSS). **Technique:** Multidetector CT scanner with intravenous iodinated contrast administered via power injector (120 mL nonionic contrast, rate 3–4 mL/sec). Arterial phase images obtained through thorax followed by portal venous phase acquisition covering abdomen and pelvis. Slice thickness 1.25 mm with multiplanar reconstructions (coronal and sagittal). --- ### FINDINGS #### Thorax / Lung Parenchyma - **Pulmonary Nodules:** Multiple bilateral solid nodular opacities ranging from 4 mm to 12 mm in greatest axial dimension. Distribution is random without predilection for upper lobes. No cavitation, calcification, or fat density observed. No associated pleural effusion or lymphadenopathy beyond mediastinal stations discussed below. The pattern is most consistent with metastatic deposits. - **Airways/Bronchi:** Patent tracheobronchial tree; no endobronchial masses or obstruction. - **Pleura:** No thickening or effusions. #### Mediastinum / Hilar Structures - **Hilar/Lymph Nodes:** Mildly enlarged right hilar node measuring ~1.2 cm short axis; otherwise unremarkable. #### Upper Abdomen - **Colon:** An ill‑defined, circumferential soft tissue mass arising from the proximal ascending colon measures approximately **6.4 cm** (craniocaudal) × 4.8 cm (transverse) × 5.2 cm (anteroposterior). The lesion demonstrates heterogeneous attenuation with areas of low density suggestive of necrosis. There is adjacent mesenteric stranding extending into pericolonic fat. No evidence of perforation or abscess formation. - **Mesenteric/Vascular Involvement:** Enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes noted along vascular pedicles (station 12—interaortocaval region, and station 13—paraaortic region) up to 1.8 cm in short-axis diameter. Vessels appear patent; no encasement visualized. - **Liver:** Normal contour and homogeneous parenchymal attenuation. No focal hypoattenuating lesions detected throughout both lobes. Portal veins normal caliber. - **Gallbladder/Biliary Tree:** Unremarkable; gallbladder distended but wall thin, no stones. Common bile duct measured ≤6 mm. - **Pancreas/Spleen/Kidneys:** All demonstrate normal morphology and attenuation. No cystic or solid lesions identified. Bilateral kidneys show preserved cortical thickness; no hydronephrosis. #### Lower Abdomen/Pelvis - **Small Bowels:** Small bowel loops uniformly collapsed appropriate to fasting state; no obstructive dilatation. - **Bladder/Prostate/Urethra:** Bladder partially filled, smooth walls, no intraluminal mass. Prostatic gland appears mildly enlarged (≈35 g) without suspicious lesion. - **Osseous Structures:** Visualized vertebral bodies, ribs, sternum, and pelvic bones exhibit normal trabecular pattern; no lytic or sclerotic lesions identified. - **Vascular Structures:** Aorta and major branches display expected calibers without aneurysm or dissection. Inferior vena cava patency maintained. --- ### IMPRESSION 1. **Primary colonic neoplasm:** Large, heterogeneously enhancing mass in the ascending colon (~6.4 cm) with surrounding mesenteric inflammatory changes and involved regional lymph nodes (stations 12 and 13), consistent with locally advanced colorectal carcinoma. 2. **Metastatic disease:** Numerous bilateral pulmonary nodules (max 12 mm) highly suggestive of hematogenous spread. No detectable hepatic metastases at this time. 3. **Additional findings:** No acute intra‑abdominal abnormality; cardiovascular structures unremarkable. TASK: Extract radiation therapy information. Include ONLY first course radiation treatment.

1. RADIATION DATE: Date radiation therapy started (YYYYMMDD).

3. RADIATION PHASES: Radiation may have up to 3 phases. Each phase has: dose per fraction, number of fractions, total dose, treatment modality, planning technique, treatment volume.

5. MODALITY: Photons, electrons, protons, IMRT, stereotactic, brachytherapy, etc.

Three tan–gray cores of firm tissue submitted in formalin, labeled “right maxillary sinus.” Total aggregate dimensions: **12 mm** in greatest linear dimension. Tissue appears gritty, without obvious necrotic debris. All specimens placed in cassettes A‑C, processed routinely, embedded in paraffin, and stained with hematoxylin & eosin (H&E). ### Microscopic Examination
*Hematoxylin & Eosin:* Sections reveal sheets and nests of markedly atypical epithelioid cells infiltrating the underlying lamina propria. Tumor cells display abundant amphophilic cytoplasm, vesicular nuclei with prominent nucleoli, and conspicuous cellular pleomorphism. Frequent mitoses (>10/10 HPF) are observed, along with occasional binucleation. Focal areas show pagetoid spread along the respiratory epithelium. No overt keratinization or gland formation is seen. Margins cannot be assessed definitively owing to the limited nature of the biopsy.

|------|--------|
| **S100 protein (IHC)** | Diffuse strong nuclear and cytoplasmic positivity in virtually all tumor cells |
| **HMB‑45 (melanoma marker)** | Strong granular cytoplasmic staining in ≥90% of cells |
| **MART‑1 (Melan-A) (IHC)** | Uniform intense cytoplasmic positivity |
| **Ki‑67 proliferative index** | Approximately 35% of tumor nuclei positive |

Interpretation of the above immunostains confirms unequivocal melanocytic lineage.

*Molecular Testing*: Comprehensive next‑generation sequencing (NGS) panel ordered separately; results pending.

### Diagnosis
1. **Malignant Melanoma, mucosal (sinonasal) origin**, epithelioid variant — highly pleomorphic, high mitotic rate.  
   • Positive for S100, HMB‑45, MART‑1 → supports melanocytic differentiation.  
   • High Ki‑67 labeling index suggests biologically aggressive behavior.

### Comments

### PATIENT INFORMATION  
**Name:** James Lee  **MRN:** [Redacted]  **Sex/Age:** Male / 68 years  

### SPECIMEN DETAILS  
| Item                     | Description                                            |
|--------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| Specimen ID              | SINUS‑001                                               |

| Tissue Source            | Right maxillary sinus (primary tumor)                  |
| Procedure                | Endoscopic core needle biopsy                          |
| Fixative                 | Formalin‐fixed paraffin‑embedded (FFPE) block         |
| Block Identifier         | FFPE‑B12345                                             |

### TEST ORDERED  
Comprehensive genomic profiling utilizing the **MSK‑Impact™ Hybrid Capture Assay (Version 4)** covering 468 cancer‑relevant genes.

### METHOD SUMMARY  
1. **DNA Extraction:** Manual macrodissection of ≥20% neoplastic cellularity; DNA isolated via Qiagen QIAamp kit.  
2. **Library Preparation & Enrichment:** Dual‑indexed libraries prepared; target enrichment performed with custom biotinylated probes spanning coding exons ± intronic splice sites of selected genes.  
3. **Sequencing Platform:** Illumina NovaSeq 6000, paired‑end 150 bp reads; mean unique depth ≈ 800× across targets.  
4. **Bioinformatic Pipeline:** Alignment to hg19 (GRCh37); duplicate marking, base quality recalibration; somatic SNV/indel calling (MuTect2), CNV determination (CNVkit), structural rearrangements (Manta). Variant allele frequency (VAF) threshold set at ≥ 5% for SNVs/Indels; copy‑number gain defined as log₂ ratio > 0.58 (≈ ≥ 3‑fold).  
5. **Quality Metrics:** % bases ≥ Q30 = 92%; uniformity (> 0.2X median) = 96%. All QC parameters met acceptance criteria.

### GENOMIC FINDINGS  

#### Somatic Single‑Nucleotide Variants / Indels  
| Gene   | Alteration (HGVS)                               | Protein Change               | VAF (%) | Interpretation |
|--------|-----------------------------------------------|------------------------------|---------|----------------|
| **KIT**    | c.1649_1670del (exon 11)                       | p.(Lys550_Glu560del)        | 38      | Activating in‑frame deletion affecting juxtamembrane domain; known sensitizing alteration for KIT TKIs. |
| **NRAS**   | c.181_183dup (exon 2) → c.182A>C               | p.Gln61Lys                   | 27      | Classic hotspot activating mutation driving MAPK signaling. |
| **TPR​53** | c.742G>A                                      | p.Arg248Gln                  | 22      | Missense change disrupting DNA binding; pathogenic. |
| **TERT**   | c.–124C>T (promoter)                           | −124C>T                      | 44      | Recurrent promoter mutation increasing telomerase expression. |

*All above variants classified as “Pathogenic” according to ACMG/AMP guidelines and COSMIC database entries.*

#### Copy‑Number Alterations  
| Gene       | CNA Status           | Approximate Fold‑Change |
|------------|----------------------|--------------------------|
| **CDKN2A** | Homozygous loss     | —                        |
| **CCND1**  | Amplification       | ~7‑fold (log₂ ratio ≈ 1.8) |
| **MDM2**   | Amplification       | ~10‑fold (log₂ ratio ≈ 2.3) |

#### Other Biomarkers  
- **Microsatellite Instability (MSI):** Stable (MSI‑S) – evaluated by 12 mononucleotide markers.  
- **Tumor Mutational Burden (TMB):** 6 mutations/Mb (low–intermediate range).  

No clinically significant fusions or other structural variants detected.

### INTERPRETION  

This sinonasal malignant melanoma harbors multiple actionable and prognostically informative alterations:

1. **KIT Exon 11 Deletion** – An established activating lesion conferring susceptibility to ATP‑competitive KIT tyrosine kinase inhibitors (e.g., imatinib, nilotinib, avapritinib). Such mutations occur preferentially in mucosal melanomas and represent the most frequent KIT aberration in this subtype.

2. **NRAS Q61K Mutation** – Drives constitutive MAPK pathway activity. While NRAS‑mutant melanoma lacks FDA‑approved targeted agents, downstream MEK inhibition has shown modest efficacy in clinical trials. Co‑existence of KIT and NRAS alterations is uncommon but reported in mucosal disease and may influence responsiveness to both KIT‑directed and immune strategies.

3. **TP53 R248Q** – Loss‑of‑function missense mutation contributing to genomic instability; commonly observed across solid tumors.

4. **TERT Promoter ‑124C>T** – Enhances telomerase transcription, supporting immortalization; frequently seen in cutaneous and mucosal melanomas.

5. **Copy‑Number Gains (CCND1, MDM2)** – Suggest cell‑cycle dysregulation through cyclin D1 up‑regulation and p53 antagonism respectively. Both alterations have been linked to aggressive behavior and reduced sensitivity to certain chemotherapeutics.

6. **CDKN2A Homozygous Deletion** – Eliminates p16INK4a function, further promoting unchecked proliferation.

Overall, the tumor exhibits a relatively low TMB (6 mut/Mb) and remains microsatellite stable, factors historically correlated with diminished responses to checkpoint inhibitor monotherapy compared with high‑TMB/MSI‑H counterparts. Nonetheless, the concurrent presence of an activated KIT driver provides a rational basis for consideration of KIT‑targeted therapy when indicated.

### LIMITATIONS  

- Analysis limited to DNA‑based alterations covered by the 468‑gene panel; RNA fusion partners outside the captured regions were not assessed.  
- Sensitivity for detecting subclonal variants below 5% VAF is limited.  
- Structural variations larger than 10 kb may escape detection without dedicated assays.

### CONCLUSION  

- **Pathogenic KIT exon 11 in‑frame deletion** (activating)  
- **Activating NRAS Q61K mutation**  
- **TP53 R248Q**, **TERT promoter –124C>T**  
- **High‑level CCND1 and MDM2 amplifications**  
- **Homozygous loss of CDKN2A**  
- **MSI‑Stable**, **TMB = 6 mut/Mb**

These findings provide comprehensive molecular insight into the biology of Mr. Lee’s sinonasal melanoma and identify potentially targetable alterations, particularly the KIT exon 11 deletion.

Clinical text (dates: 254926 to 254935):
---
=== Clinical Note dated 254926 ===
**Pathology Report**

---

**Specimen Identification:**  
- **Accession #:** OV-2025-0701  
- **Patient Name / MRN:** Linda Thompson / ***[Redacted]***  
- **Date of Collection:** *[date omitted]*  

**Clinical Information:**  
- 70‑year‑old woman with radiologic evidence of a large bilateral adnexal mass and suspected peritoneal carcinomatosis. Pre‑operative impression: ovarian malignancy, probable high‑grade serous carcinoma.  

**Procedure(s):**  
- Exploratory laparotomy with bilateral salpingo‑ovariectomy, total abdominal hysterectomy, infracolic omentectomy, and sampling of peritoneal surfaces. Specimens submitted intact and in separate containers as indicated below.  

**Gross Description:**  

| Container | Tissue Submitted | Measurements (cm) | Appearance |
|-----------|------------------|-------------------|------------|
| Ovary L   | Left ovary + attached tube | 13 × 9 × 8 | External capsule irregularly thickened; cut surface reveals multiloculated cystic spaces filled with hemorrhagic fluid interspersed with firm tan-white solid areas. Numerous adherent fibrinous plaques on serosal surface. |
| Ovary R   | Right ovary + attached tube | 12 × 8 × 7 | Similar appearance to left side; dominant solid component occupying ≈60 % of volume, gritty texture, focal necrotic foci. Surface studded with ≤2‑mm grayish nodules. |
| Uterus    | Corpus & cervix (intact)      | 9 × 6 × 4 | Myometrium unremarkable. Endometrial cavity empty. No obvious intramural lesions. |
| Omentum   | Infracolic omentum            | 15 × 10 × 2 (rolled) | Diffuse “cake”–like infiltration throughout thickness; pale yellow-tan rubbery consistency. |
| Peritoneal Washings | Ascitic fluid collected intraoperatively | – | Sent for cytology. |

All specimens were inked where appropriate, fixed in neutral buffered formalin, processed routinely, embedded in paraffin, and stained with hematoxylin‑eosin (H&E). Additional unstained slides prepared for immunohistochemical (IHC) studies.

**Microscopic Examination:**  

*Left Ovary:* Sections show replacement of normal ovarian parenchyma by infiltrative nests and sheets of markedly pleomorphic epithelioid cells forming complex papillae with hierarchical branching. Nuclear features include prominent nucleoli, coarse chromatin clumping, and frequent mitoses (>25/10 high power fields). Areas of necrosis and psammoma bodies are present. Tumor extends through the cortical stroma to involve the serosal surface (serosal breach confirmed). 

*Right Ovary:* Identical morphology to left ovary with similar high‑grade features and serosal involvement. Focal luteinized stromal reaction adjacent to tumor noted.

*Uterus:* Cervical and endometrial mucosa uninvolved. Myometrial tissue free of tumor. No direct extension observed.

*Omentum:* Extensive metastatic deposits composed of identical high‑grade serous carcinoma replacing adipose lobules. Desmoplastic stromal reaction evident. Margins of sampled omental fat appear fully replaced by tumor.

*Cytology (peritoneal washings):* Scattered clusters of malignant cells exhibiting high nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, hyperchromatic nuclei, and occasional macronucleoli compatible with serous adenocarcinoma.

**Immunohistochemistry (selected panel):**  

| Marker | Result | Interpretation |
|--------|--------|----------------|
| WT1    | Strong diffuse nuclear positivity | Supports Müllerian origin |
| PAX8   | Positive (nuclear)               | Consistent with gynecologic lineage |
| Cytokeratin 7 (CK7) | Positive          | Typical for serous carcinoma |
| p53    | Aberrant pattern – overexpression (“null” vs “missense”) | Correlates with TP53 missense mutation |
| Ki‑67  | Approximately 78 % of tumor nuclei labeled | Indicates high proliferative index |
| ER     | Negative                         | Common in high‑grade serous subtype |
| PR     | Negative                         | — |
| HER2 (by IHC) | Score 0                     | Not amplified |

Additional molecular testing (NGS) has been ordered separately; results pending.

**Diagnosis (Final):**  

1. **High‑Grade Serous Carcinoma, Ovary**, bilateral, with extensive serosal involvement and omental metastasis.  
2. **Stage IIIC** (FIGO/AJCC 8th edition) – T3c, N1 (positive peritoneal nodes implied by omental spread), M0.  

**Comments:**   
- Histopathologic features are classic for high‑grade serous carcinoma of ovarian origin.  
- The aberrant p53 IHC correlates with known TP53 hotspot mutations frequently seen in this entity.  
- Molecular profiling recommended per institutional guidelines to assess for homologous recombination deficiency (BRCA1/2 status) and potential eligibility for targeted agents.  

*(Report generated by Department of Anatomic Pathology)*

=== Clinical Note dated 254927 ===
**Imaging Report**

---

### Patient Information  
- **Name:** Linda Thompson  
- **Age/Sex:** 70‑year‑old Female  

### Study Details  
- **Modality:** Computed Tomography (CT) – Abdomen & Pelvis with Intravenous Contrast  
- **Technique:** Multidetector helical acquisition performed during a single breath‑hold series. Images obtained axial plane with reconstructions in coronal and sagittal planes. IV non‑ionic iodinated contrast administered (approximately 100 mL at 3–4 mL/sec) with portal venous phase timing (≈70 seconds post‑injection). Slice thickness 2.5 mm; reconstruction kernel soft tissue algorithm. Oral positive contrast was not utilized.  

--- 

## Findings  

| Anatomic Region | Description |
|-----------------|-------------|
| **Ovaries / Adnexa** | Bilateral markedly enlarged ovaries coalescing into a complex solid/cystic mass measuring up to **12 cm** in greatest dimension (right > left). The masses demonstrate heterogeneous attenuation with areas of necrosis, papillary projections, and irregular thickened septa. There is loss of normal fat planes surrounding both adnexa. |
| **Uterus** | Normal size uterus with unremarkable myometrial signal. Endometrium appears thin and homogeneous. No focal uterine lesion identified. |
| **Fallopian Tubes** | Not separately visualized due to confluent tumor burden involving adjacent structures. |
| **Peritoneum / Omentum** | Prominent “omental cake” pattern characterized by diffuse soft‑tissue infiltration of the greater omentum extending inferiorly toward the transverse colon mesentery. Measured thickness ≈ 2.5 cm. Numerous small (<1 cm) enhancing peritoneal nodules scattered throughout the supracolic compartment. |
| **Pelvic Implants** | Multiple discrete soft‑tissue implants noted along the posterior cul-de-sac, lateral pelvic sidewalls, and bladder dome. Largest implant measures **3.2 cm** in short axis located at the right pelvic sidewall. All lesions enhance avidly following contrast administration. |
| **Mesenteric Nodes** | Several mildly enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes (short-axis ≤ 7 mm) observed; however, none meet conventional criteria for pathologic enlargement (>10 mm). |
| **Retroperitoneal Lymphadenopathy** | Small para-aortic and iliac chain nodes up to **1.0 cm** in short axis; borderline but not definitively abnormal. |
| **Upper abdomen** | Liver demonstrates homogenous parenchymal density without focal hypoattenuating lesions. Spleen, pancreas, adrenal glands appear unremarkable. No evidence of hepatic capsular retraction or biliary dilatation. |
| **Thoracic Upper Abdomen** | Lower lungs partially captured; no obvious pulmonary nodules or pleural effusion. Diaphragmatic domes intact. |
| **Bowel** | Loops of small bowel displaced superiorly by massive adnexal mass; wall thickness preserved, no obstruction evident. Colon shows mild luminal narrowing secondary to external compression near sigmoid region but remains patent. |
| **Bone Window Review** | Visualized osseous structures show no lytic or sclerotic lesions suggestive of metastatic disease. |

*No free intraperitoneal fluid detected.*  

--- 

## Impression  

1. Large (**~12 cm**) bilateral ovarian/adnexal mass highly suspicious for high‑grade serous epithelial ovarian carcinoma, correlating with recent pathological diagnosis.  
2. Extensive peritoneal carcinomatosis manifested as classic omental caking and numerous pelvic/peritoneal implants—measurable intra‑abdominal disease meeting RECIST target lesion criteria.  
3. Regional lymph nodes equivocal; no definitive distant metastases identified in upper abdominal viscera or skeletal survey.  

Overall staging compatible with advanced FIGO Stage III‑C disease (T3c, N1, M0). Further multidisciplinary discussion recommended for optimal neoadjuvant systemic therapy planning.

=== Clinical Note dated 254928 ===
**Oncology Progress Note – Restaging Evaluation**

---

### Patient  
Linda Thompson, 70‑year‑old female  

---  

#### Chief Complaint  
Follow‑up appointment to review restaging computed tomography performed after three cycles of neoadjuvant carboplatin/paclitaxel.

---  

#### History of Present Illness  
Ms. Thompson was diagnosed six months ago with FIGO Stage IIIC high‑grade serous epithelial ovarian carcinoma (T3c N1 M0). She subsequently initiated neoadjuvant systemic therapy consisting of carboplatin dosed at AUC 5 and paclitaxel 175 mg/m² administered intravenously every 21 days. She tolerated the first three cycles well, reporting mild fatigue and occasional nausea controlled with ondansetron; no neuropathy, alopecia, or hematologic complications were noted beyond grade 1 neutropenia that resolved spontaneously.

1. CHEMO DATE: Date chemotherapy started (YYYYMMDD).
2. RX SUMM--CHEMO: 00=none, 01=chemo NOS, 02=single agent, 03=multi-agent, 82=chemo recommended unknown if given, 85=chemo not recommended, 86=chemo contraindicated, 87=patient refused, 88=patient died, 99=unknown.

Susan Patel is a 69‑year‑old woman with a remote history of left‐sided clear‑cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) status post radical nephrectomy (pT3b N0, Fuhrman Grade 3 with sarcomatoid features) completed 13 months ago. She was transitioned to frontline axitinib 5 mg PO BID shortly thereafter. Over the ensuing months she tolerated axitinib with manageable grade 2 diarrhoea and grade 1 hand–foot skin reaction. Given radiographic progression and intolerance to continued VEGF‑TKI therapy, the multidisciplinary tumor board recommended initiation of immunotherapy with pembrolizumab monotherapy (200 mg IV q3wks). Unfortunately, the patient’s candidacy for several active phase II/III checkpoint inhibitor trials is precluded owing to prior exposure to a VEGF‑TKI (adjuvant sunitinib) and documented disease progression within 12 months of completing adjuvant therapy—a stipulated exclusion criterion. Nonetheless, standard FDA‑approved pembrolizumab for advanced/metastatic RCC remains available outside a trial setting.

During counseling, Ms. Patel expressed understanding of the rationale for switching to PD‑1 blockade, voiced concerns regarding potential immune‑related toxicities (e.g., hepatitis, colitis, pneumonitis), and affirmed willingness to proceed with pembrolizumab as best systemic option at this juncture.

1. **Metastatic clear‑cell renal cell carcinoma**, refractory to sequential VEGF‑targeted TKIs (sunitinib → axitinib). Molecular profile demonstrates VHL splice‑site alteration, multiple chromatin‐modifying gene losses (PBRM1, BAP1) and PTEN loss—all associated with aggressive biology and poorer response to checkpoint inhibition. Currently limited systemic options; enrollment in most active trials precluded by prior VEGF‑TKI exposure and rapid recurrence timeline.  

2. **Functional decline** – ECOG 2, increasing dependence on caregiver support, intermittent dyspnea, moderate fatigue, and psychosocial distress concerning prognosis.  

3. **Hepatic dysfunction** – Transaminases ≈2 × ULN, likely multifactorial (tumour infiltrative vs underlying hepatitis C sequelae). Limits tolerability of many systemic agents and influences anticoagulant metabolism.  

4. **Deep‑Vein Thrombosis** – On therapeutic enoxaparin; no bleeding complications thus far.  

5. **Hypertension** – Well-controlled on lisinopril; monitor closely if anti‑angiogenic therapy reinitiated.  

6. **Symptomatic burdens** – Diarrhea (residual from prior axitinib), mild nausea, hand‑foot skin toxicity largely resolved, anxiety/depressed mood.

**A. Immediate Symptom Management**

2. **Diarrhea/Nausea:** Continue ondansetron 4 mg ODT PRN; start diphenoxylate‑atropine 5 mg PO bid for persistent stool frequency >3/day. Monitor electrolytes weekly.  
3. **Hand‑Foot Syndrome:** Apply urea‑based emollient twice daily; avoid friction; consider topical clobetasol 0.05% once nightly if inflammation recurs.  
4. **Anxiety/Depression:** Offer counseling referral; screen PHQ‑9; initiate sertraline 25 mg PO daily if depressive scores ≥10, after confirming no serotonergic interaction with existing meds.

- Discuss possibility of initiating immune checkpoint inhibitor combination (nivolumab + ipilimumab) *off‑label*, acknowledging limited data in heavily pre‑treated VHL‑altered tumors and potential hepatic toxicities. Obtain informed consent outlining risks/benefits.

**D. Hepatology Follow‑up**  
- Schedule appointment within 1 week to optimize hepatitis C management (consider direct‑acting antiviral course) and address transaminitis. Evaluate need for hepatoprotective measures (e.g., ursodeoxycholic acid).

- Refer to social work for financial/caregiver resources, transportation aid, and community support groups for metastatic RCC.  
- Offer spiritual care chaplaincy consultation upon request.

- Return clinic visit in 1 week for symptom check, medication reconciliation, and review of laboratory trends.  
- Reassess imaging in 8 weeks unless clinically indicated sooner (e.g., acute decompensation).

- **Sequencing Depth:** Median unique depth ≥800× across target regions.

### Detected Genomic Alterations  

| Gene | Variant(s) | Molecular Consequence | Allele Frequency* | Interpretation |
|------|------------|-----------------------|-------------------|---------------|
| **SMARCA4** | *Biallelic deletion* (exons 1‑31 lost) | Loss of function → SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex disruption | — (copy‑neutral loss) | Consistent with SMARCA4‑deficient (“SWI/SNF‑mut”) thoracic adenocarcinoma; associated with aggressive phenotype. |

| **STK11** | c.1060T>C (p.F354L) | Predicted loss‑of‑function (LOF) | 32% | Co‑mutation with KRAS linked to poorer outcomes and reduced responsiveness to PD‑1 blockade. |

1. **Oncogenic Drivers** – The tumor harbors multiple activating alterations in the Ras/Raf/MEK pathway (KRAS G12D, NF1 loss, STK11 LOF). This constellation drives constitutive downstream signaling and underlies the observed aggressive behavior. Presence of KRAS G12D precludes efficacy of EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors.

2. **SMARCA4 Deficiency** – Complete loss of SMARCA4 protein correlates with “SMARCA4‑deficient” NSCLC, a subset characterized by high-grade morphology, propensity for early dissemination, and limited sensitivity to conventional chemotherapy.

3. **MET Amplification** – A seven‑fold gain exceeds most institutional cutoffs for potential MET‑targeted therapy (e.g., crizo, tepotinib, savolitinib). Confirmation via orthogonal method (e.g., FISH) is advisable before enrollment into MET‑focused trials.

- The assay interrogates DNA alterations only; RNA fusion partners were not assessed.  
- Subclonal populations below the detection threshold (<5% VAF) could remain undetected.  
- Functional impact of certain missense changes (e.g., STK11 F354L) inferred from computational predictions; confirmatory functional assays unavailable.

- Consider confirmation of MET amplification by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) or quantitative PCR.

TASK: Extract chemotherapy, hormone therapy, immunotherapy (BRM), and other systemic treatment.

CRITICAL RULES:
1. CHEMO DATE: Date chemotherapy started (YYYYMMDD).
2. RX SUMM--CHEMO: 00=none, 01=chemo NOS, 02=single agent, 03=multi-agent, 82=chemo recommended unknown if given, 85=chemo not recommended, 86=chemo contraindicated, 87=patient refused, 88=patient died, 99=unknown.

### Test Ordered  
Comprehensive Next‑Generation Sequencing (NGS) panel for hematologic malignancies covering DNA‐based mutation detection, copy number variation (CNV) analysis, RNA‑fusion discovery, and expression profiling (including CRLF2).

### Methodology Summary  
- **DNA & RNA extraction:** Automated magnetic bead–based isolation (Qiagen).  
- **Library preparation:** Hybrid‑capture enrichment (Illumina TruSight Oncology 500); separate cDNA synthesis for fusion/transcript quantification.  
- **Sequencing platform:** Illumina NovaSeq 6000, paired‑end 150 bp reads.  
- **Coverage statistics:** Median depth ≥ 800× across target regions; >99% bases covered at ≥30×.  
- **Bioinformatic pipeline:** Alignment to hg38, variant calling with Mutect2 (SNVs/indels), CNVkit (copy‑number), STAR‑Fusion (RNA fusions), normalized read count for gene expression.  
- **Analytical sensitivity:** Detectable allelic fraction ≥ 2% for SNVs/indels; ≥ 5% for structural variants.

### Genomic Findings  

| Alteration                              | Variant Class            | Allele Frequency* | Clinical Significance* |
|----------------------------------------|---------------------------|-------------------|-------------------------|
| **BCR‑ABL1 fusion (e13a2)**             | Gene Fusion (p190 protein) | Detected (RNA)    | Pathogenic – hallmark of Philadelphia‑positive ALL; confers constitutive ABL1 TK activity. |
| **IKZF1 exon 4‑7 deletion**            | Homozygous Deletion (CNV) | —                 | Adverse prognostic marker in Ph⁺ B‑ALL; linked to steroid resistance. |
| **CDKN2A/CDKN2B homozygous loss**       | Homozygous Deletion (CNV) | —                 | Tumor suppressor loss; associated with aggressive phenotype. |
| **CRLF2 overexpression**                | mRNA Upregulation         | ≈ 8‑fold ↑ vs normal control | Suggestive of JAK‑STAT pathway activation; seen in “Ph‑like” subset but co‑exists here. |
| **KRAS G12D**                           | Missense SNV              | 15%               | Activating MAPK pathway mutation; contributes to leukemogenesis. |
| **NRAS Q61K**                           | Missense SNV              | 9%                | Co‑occurring activating RAS mutation; similar functional impact as KRAS. |
| **PTPN11 E69K**                         | Missense SNV              | 6%                | Gain‑of‑function phosphatase affecting downstream signaling; reported in acute leukemia. |

\*Allele frequency reflects proportion of mutated reads among total informative reads (applicable to SNVs/Indels). Copy‑number changes are reported qualitatively.

### Interpretative Commentary  

The comprehensive genomic profile confirms classic Philadelphia chromosome positivity through detection of the BCR‑ABL1 p190 transcript, establishing the diagnosis of Ph⁺ B‑ALL. Concomitant IKZF1 deletion and biallelic loss of CDKN2A/B denote a high‑risk genetic backdrop frequently correlated with inferior response to standard chemotherapy regimens. Overexpression of CRLF2 raises the possibility of synergistic JAK‑STAT signaling, although no accompanying JAK2 rearrangement was observed.

Activating lesions in KRAS, NRAS, and PTPN11 collectively indicate robust MAPK pathway engagement, potentially contributing to disease persistence despite targeted ABL inhibition. While these RAS‑pathway mutations are less typical in isolated Ph⁺ cases, their presence underscores biologic heterogeneity and may influence future therapeutic considerations such as incorporation of MEK inhibitors—though such decisions lie outside the scope of this report.

Overall, the detected aberrations delineate a complex mutational landscape characteristic of high‑risk adult B‑ALL and provide essential baseline data for longitudinal minimal residual disease (MRD) tracking and potential enrollment into genotype‑directed clinical trials.

### Report Limitations  

- Sensitivity limited to ≥ 2% VAF for single nucleotide variants; subclonal events below this threshold may remain undetected.  
- Structural variations other than targeted fusions (e.g., cryptic insertions) are not comprehensively assessed.  
- Expression levels derived from bulk RNA; tumor purity influences quantitative accuracy.

### History of Present Illness  

Susan Patel is a 69‑year‑old woman with a remote history of left‐sided clear‑cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) status post radical nephrectomy (pT3b N0, Fuhrman Grade 3 with sarcomatoid features) completed 13 months ago. She received adjuvant sunitinib for 12 months, complicated by grade 3 fatigue/anorexia requiring dose reduction and transient grade 2 hypertension now controlled on lisinopril 20 mg daily. After completion of adjuvant therapy, surveillance imaging at month 10 uncovered a 1.8 cm right lower lobe pulmonary nodule and a 1.2 cm segment VIII hepatic lesion. Biopsy of the liver confirmed metastatic ccRCC; subsequent NGS disclosed VHL splice‑site alteration, PBRM1 missense, BAP1 truncation, PTEN loss, CDKN2A homozygous deletion, TMB 2.8 mut/Mb, MSS.

She was transitioned to frontline axitinib 5 mg PO BID shortly thereafter. Over the ensuing months she tolerated axitinib with manageable grade 2 diarrhoea and grade 1 hand–foot skin reaction. Approximately three weeks ago (age 69) laboratory work demonstrated worsening transaminases (ALT 2.0 × ULN, AST 1.9 × ULN) attributed to axitinib toxicity; the agent was held pending re‑evaluation. Repeat contrast‑enhanced CT of chest/abdomen today shows modest growth of the hepatic lesion to 1.5 cm (previously 1.2 cm) with the pulmonary nodule unchanged at 1.8 cm — overall pattern compatible with slowly progressive disease.

Given radiographic progression and intolerance to continued VEGF‑TKI therapy, the multidisciplinary tumor board recommended initiation of immunotherapy with pembrolizumab monotherapy (200 mg IV q3wks). Unfortunately, the patient’s candidacy for several active phase II/III checkpoint inhibitor trials is precluded owing to prior exposure to a VEGF‑TKI (adjuvant sunitinib) and documented disease progression within 12 months of completing adjuvant therapy—a stipulated exclusion criterion. Nonetheless, standard FDA‑approved pembrolizumab for advanced/metastatic RCC remains available outside a trial setting.

During counseling, Ms. Patel expressed understanding of the rationale for switching to PD‑1 blockade, voiced concerns regarding potential immune‑related toxicities (e.g., hepatitis, colitis, pneumonitis), and affirmed willingness to proceed with pembrolizumab as best systemic option at this juncture.

## Assessment  

1. **Metastatic clear‑cell renal cell carcinoma**, refractory to sequential VEGF‑targeted TKIs (sunitinib → axitinib). Molecular profile demonstrates VHL splice‑site alteration, multiple chromatin‐modifying gene losses (PBRM1, BAP1) and PTEN loss—all associated with aggressive biology and poorer response to checkpoint inhibition. Currently limited systemic options; enrollment in most active trials precluded by prior VEGF‑TKI exposure and rapid recurrence timeline.  

2. **Functional decline** – ECOG 2, increasing dependence on caregiver support, intermittent dyspnea, moderate fatigue, and psychosocial distress concerning prognosis.  

3. **Hepatic dysfunction** – Transaminases ≈2 × ULN, likely multifactorial (tumour infiltrative vs underlying hepatitis C sequelae). Limits tolerability of many systemic agents and influences anticoagulant metabolism.  

4. **Deep‑Vein Thrombosis** – On therapeutic enoxaparin; no bleeding complications thus far.  

5. **Hypertension** – Well-controlled on lisinopril; monitor closely if anti‑angiogenic therapy reinitiated.  

6. **Symptomatic burdens** – Diarrhea (residual from prior axitinib), mild nausea, hand‑foot skin toxicity largely resolved, anxiety/depressed mood.  

Overall goal shifts toward maximizing quality of life, alleviating symptoms, clarifying values/goals, and facilitating coordinated hospice planning if desired.

---  

## Plan  

**A. Immediate Symptom Management**  
1. **Pain/Fatigue:** Initiate scheduled acetaminophen 650 mg PO q6h PRN breakthrough dosing; consider low‑dose morphine sulfate 2.5 mg PO q4h PRN if pain escalates (>3/10). Encourage gentle activity pacing and daytime naps.  
2. **Diarrhea/Nausea:** Continue ondansetron 4 mg ODT PRN; start diphenoxylate‑atropine 5 mg PO bid for persistent stool frequency >3/day. Monitor electrolytes weekly.  
3. **Hand‑Foot Syndrome:** Apply urea‑based emollient twice daily; avoid friction; consider topical clobetasol 0.05% once nightly if inflammation recurs.  
4. **Anxiety/Depression:** Offer counseling referral; screen PHQ‑9; initiate sertraline 25 mg PO daily if depressive scores ≥10, after confirming no serotonergic interaction with existing meds.  

**B. Oncology Coordination**  
- Discuss possibility of initiating immune checkpoint inhibitor combination (nivolumab + ipilimumab) *off‑label*, acknowledging limited data in heavily pre‑treated VHL‑altered tumors and potential hepatic toxicities. Obtain informed consent outlining risks/benefits.  
- Alternatively, evaluate suitability for best supportive care alone versus enrolment in a biomarker‑driven basket trial accepting prior VEGF‑TKI exposure (if becomes available).  

**C. Anticoagulation**  
- Maintain therapeutic enoxaparin; assess renal function monthly; plan transition to apixaban 5 mg PO bid if creatinine clearance remains adequate and patient prefers oral regimen.  

**D. Hepatology Follow‑up**  
- Schedule appointment within 1 week to optimize hepatitis C management (consider direct‑acting antiviral course) and address transaminitis. Evaluate need for hepatoprotective measures (e.g., ursodeoxycholic acid).  

**E. Advance Care Planning**  
- Conduct structured Goals‑Of‑Care conversation focusing on: understanding of disease trajectory, preferred location of death, code status, durable power of attorney for healthcare, and specific wishes regarding mechanical ventilation/intubation. Document decisions clearly in EMR.  
- Provide educational materials on hospice benefits; arrange meeting with hospice nurse navigator within 48 hours.  

**F. Psychosocial Support**  
- Refer to social work for financial/caregiver resources, transportation aid, and community support groups for metastatic RCC.  
- Offer spiritual care chaplaincy consultation upon request.  

**G. Follow‑Up Timeline**  
- Return clinic visit in 1 week for symptom check, medication reconciliation, and review of laboratory trends.  
- Reassess imaging in 8 weeks unless clinically indicated sooner (e.g., acute decompensation).

### TEST PERFORMED
Comprehensive solid‑tumor genomic profiling utilizing a validated 511‑gene hybrid‑capture NGS panel (Commercially marketed as “OncoPanel‑511”). The assay interrogates coding regions of selected genes for base substitutions, insertions/deletions, select intronic fusions, copy‑number alterations, and limited structural rearrangements.

### METHODOLOGY SUMMARY
- Library preparation via enzymatic fragmentation & adapter ligation.  
- Target enrichment by biotinylated probe hybridization (median target coverage ≈ 550×).  
- Paired‑end sequencing on Illumina NovaSeq 6000.  
- Bioinformatic pipeline includes alignment to hg19, duplicate removal, local realignment, and variant calling (MuTect2 for SNVs/indels; CNVkit for copy‑number).  
- Variant annotation utilizes COSMIC v94, ClinVar, OncoKB, and internal curated database.  
- Analytical sensitivity: ≥5 % allelic fraction for SNVs/indels; ≥2‑copy fold change for amplifications; detection of homozygous deletions ≤1 % cellularity.

### RESULTS

#### Somatic Sequence Variants (Pathogenic / Likely Pathogenic)

| Gene | Nucleotide Change* | Protein Effect | Allele Frequency (%) | Classification |
|------|--------------------|---------------|---------------------|----------------|
| **PIK3CA** | c.3140A>G | p.His1047Arg | 27 | Pathogenic (activating) |
| **TP53**   | c.524G>T | p.Arg175His | 22 | Pathogenic (loss‑of‑function) |
| **CDH1**   | c.1799‑1G>A | Splice donor ‑1 → A (exon 13) | — | Likely pathogenic (disrupts E‑cadherin) |
| **GATA3**  | c.424_425delAG | p.Ser142Phefs*24 | 15 | Likely pathogenic (frameshift) |
| **ESR1**   | c.1610A>C | p.Tyr537Ser | 5 | Pathogenic (ligand‑binding domain mutation conferring hormone resistance) |
| **MAP3K1** | c.964G>A | p.Glu322Lys | 12 | Likely pathogenic (kinase domain) |

\*Genomic coordinates refer to NM_* transcripts according to RefSeq.

#### Copy‑Number Alterations

| Gene | Type | Approximate Fold Change |
|------|------|--------------------------|
| **CCND1** | Amplification | +4‑fold (high‑level) |
| **CDKN2A** | Homozygous Deletion | Loss of both alleles |
| **PTEN** | Low‑level loss | Relative copy number decrease (~−1.5 copies) |

- No clinically significant BRCA1/BRCA2 somatic alterations detected.

- Tumor mutational burden (TMB): 4 Mut/Mb (low).

### INTERPRETION
Emily’s tumor harbors several well‑characterized driver alterations typical of HR⁺/HER2‑negative breast cancer:

1. **PIK3CA H1047R** – Activating hotspot mutation driving PI3K‑AKT signaling; predictive of responsiveness to α‑specific PI3K inhibitors (e.g., alpelisib) when paired with endocrine therapy.  
2. **ESR1 Y537S** – Constitutively active ligand‑binding domain substitution associated with acquired resistance to aromatase inhibition; may influence choice of subsequent hormonal agents.  
3. **TP53 R175H**, **CDH1 splice-site**, **GATA3 frameshift**, and **MAP3K1 missense** collectively reflect genomic complexity and could contribute to altered differentiation and proliferative capacity.

- Testing performed on archival FFPE material; very low tumor purity (<10 %) could result in false negatives.

- Germline status cannot be assessed; separate hereditary testing required if indicated.
